Electrostatics

 Home Physics Branches of physics Electromagnetism
OurBigBook.com Words: 9k Articles: 99
Electrostatics studies time-independent electric charge distributions and their electric fields. In vacuum, its local equations in SI units are
∇⋅E=ϵ0​ρ​,∇×E=0,E=−∇Φ,∇2Φ=−ϵ0​ρ​.
(1)
Here ρ is charge density, ϵ0​ is vacuum permittivity, and Φ is electric potential. Gauss's law supplies the divergence equation; the static form of Faraday's law of induction supplies the zero curl. The Poisson equation becomes Laplace's equation where there is no electric charge. Prescribed electric charges give electric fields through Coulomb's law and the superposition principle; mobile electric charges on an electrical conductor instead require solving for their distribution together with the electric potential. [ref].
The useful distinction is between prescribed sources and prescribed boundary conditions. On a grounded electrical conductor, an external connection fixes its electric potential relative to an electrical reference potential and allows electric charge to enter or leave. On an isolated electrical conductor, total electric charge is fixed and its constant electric potential is an unknown. A neutral isolated electrical conductor can therefore have a nonzero local surface charge density through electrostatic induction. Equal electric potentials also do not imply equal electric charges: charge sharing between distant connected spheres gives a simple geometric example. [ref].
Electrostatics is useful because a spatial boundary value problem replaces the need to follow every moving charge carrier during charge relaxation. It describes the settled state of a capacitor and explains electrostatic shielding of sensitive equipment. Its assumptions must match the apparatus: stationary boundaries and sources, negligible time variation of the magnetic field, and enough time for charge relaxation. A metal carrying a maintained electric current through finite electrical resistance generally needs a nonzero internal electric field by Ohm's law; it is not a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium. Static macroscopic electric charge also does not mean that every electron is motionless. [ref].

Uniqueness of an electrostatic dielectric boundary-value problem

Words: 122 Articles: 1
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
For positive scalar permittivities and specified free charges, fixed conductor potentials, dielectric matching conditions and decay at infinity, the electrostatic field is unique. Subtract two proposed potentials and integrate ∇⋅(ϵδϕ∇δϕ). The boundary terms vanish or cancel across dielectric interfaces, leaving ∫ϵ∣∇δϕ∣2dV=0. Hence the difference field is zero, with any potential constant fixed by the boundary convention.

Uniqueness theorem for the electrostatic potential

Words: 67
Uniqueness of an electrostatic dielectric boundary-value problem OurBigBook.com
In a vacuum domain with specified charge density, fixed boundary electric potential and the appropriate condition at infinity, two solutions of the Poisson equation have difference w satisfying ∇2w=0 with zero boundary data. Integration by parts gives ∫∣∇w∣2dV=0; hence their electric fields coincide, and their potentials coincide after fixing the constant. This is the Dirichlet case of the more general dielectric uniqueness result. It justifies the exterior field constructed by the method of images.

Electrostatic screening

Words: 78
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
Mobile electric charges redistribute in response to an imposed electric potential, partly compensating its field. The induced density response and the Poisson equation must be solved self-consistently. Classical dilute mobile ions lead to the Debye–Hückel approximation; a degenerate electron system instead has a response set by its electronic compressibility and interactions. A high charge response can pin a partly occupied Landau level near the Fermi energy, whereas an incompressible gap suppresses that response. electrostatic screening is not a claim that every material perfectly excludes every static field.

Conducting-wedge potential expansion (Φ−V0​=∑n≥1​(an​rnπ/α+bn​r−nπ/α)sin(nπθ/α))

Words: 118 Articles: 1
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
In a charge-free wedge 0<θ<α bounded by equal-potential conductor faces, separation of Laplace's equation gives the displayed local harmonic expansion. Bounded potential at a finite corner removes negative powers. Outer boundary conditions determine the remaining coefficients; the conductor potential alone does not determine a nonconstant solution in an unbounded domain.

Electrostatic corner-field exponent (E∼rπ/α−1)

Words: 70
Conducting-wedge potential expansion OurBigBook.com
If the lowest allowed angular harmonic has a nonzero coefficient, differentiating its potential gives the displayed field scale. The field vanishes at a right-angle recess, stays finite at a smooth face, and diverges at a protruding conducting corner whose exterior vacuum angle exceeds π. A rounded tip cuts off the ideal power law at its radius scale. If the first coefficient vanishes, the first nonzero higher harmonic determines the exponent instead.

Electrostatic pressure (pe​=E⋅D/2)

Words: 55
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
The outward normal electric traction on an equipotential conductor adjoining a linear isotropic dielectric, for the ideal normal-field configuration, is pe​=ϵEn2​/2=E⋅D/2. Integrating this normal traction over a surface gives the electric force. It is a field-stress contribution; mechanical pressure and dielectric boundary conditions must be included when determining an actual fluid-interface equilibrium.

Half-immersed conducting sphere in a dielectric (V=Q/[2πϵ0​(1+ϵr​)a])

Words: 99
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
An equipotential sphere centred in a flat interface between vacuum and a linear dielectric admits the same potential C/r in both media. The radial field is tangential at the interface, so tangential E and normal D boundary conditions are satisfied. Displacement flux through the hemispheres gives Q=2πϵ0​(1+ϵr​)C, yielding the displayed sphere potential. E has equal magnitude at equal radius; D and free surface charge are larger by ϵr​ on the dielectric side.
Integrating electrostatic pressure gives a force toward the dielectric of magnitude Q2(ϵr​−1)/[8πϵ0​(1+ϵr​)2a2]. A deforming liquid interface or surface tension needs additional mechanical conditions beyond this ideal flat-interface solution.

Conducting sphere

Words: 31
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
A spherical electrical conductor has constant electric potential throughout its connected interior in electrostatic equilibrium. For an isolated sphere in a homogeneous medium, spherical symmetry and Gauss's law give the exterior field of a point electric charge at its center.

Potential of an inverse-radius spherical charge density

Words: 38
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
A charge cloud ρ=A/r for 0<r<a encloses Q(r)=2πAr2. With no central point charge and potential zero at infinity, Gauss's law gives ϕ=A(2a−r)/(2ϵ0​) inside and Aa2/(2ϵ0​r) outside. The density singularity is integrable, and the potential is finite at the origin.

Electric double layer

Words: 679 Articles: 15
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
An electric double layer consists of an interfacial electric charge and the compensating distribution of mobile ions in the adjacent chemical solution. Counterions are enriched and coions depleted near a simple charged interface. A diffuse layer is described approximately by the Poisson-Boltzmann equation; a compact specifically adsorbed layer requires additional surface chemistry. Overlap of diffuse layers can produce a screened repulsion between like-charged colloids.

Charge regulation

Words: 54
Electric double layer OurBigBook.com
A surface can change its surface charge density as its local electric potential and solution composition change, for example through reversible ionization or ion adsorption. This couples the surface reaction equilibrium to the surrounding electric double layer. Fixed-charge and fixed-potential models are limiting boundary conditions rather than interchangeable descriptions. Salt or pH changes can therefore alter both electrostatic screening and the repulsion amplitude.

Overcompensation of an initial interfacial charge by adsorbed species or correlated ions, so the charge or potential inferred outside the compact interfacial region has the opposite sign. Screening of a fixed boundary charge alone is not the same mechanism.

Electro-osmosis

Words: 327 Articles: 5
Electric double layer OurBigBook.com
Electro-osmosis is fluid motion driven by an applied electric field acting on mobile electric charge near a surface. A charged interface attracts a diffuse population of counterions in an electric double layer. A field component tangent to the interface exerts a force density ρe​E on that mobile charge; momentum transfer to the surrounding solvent drives flow opposed by viscous stress. In a capillary electrophoresis measurement, this flow advects the sample as well as its electrical drift relative to the fluid. Locally, the measured axial velocity is vobserved​=ueo​+μep​E, where ueo​ is the electroosmotic fluid velocity and μep​ is the electrophoretic mobility. [ref]

Uniform wall charge and polymer entry scaling

Words: 59
Electro-osmosis OurBigBook.com
A homogeneous charged channel can add a constant electro-osmotic drift to the ideal electrophoretic velocity at fixed field. It changes the coefficient of a linear length-versus-entry-time law without generating a new length exponent. Charge-dependent adsorption, heterogeneous trapping or cancellation of drift followed by diffusion lies outside that simple claim; wall charge cannot be excluded as an indirect cause in every real experiment.

Electro-osmosis OurBigBook.com
With ψ(0)=ζ, ψ′(d)=0 and no slip at either wall, linear screening gives ψ/ζ=cosh[κ(d−x)]/cosh(κd). The velocity is v/U=1−(1−sechκd)x/d−cosh[κ(d−x)]/cosh(κd). This electrically neutral-wall boundary assumes no external normal field; it differs from a grounded wall.

Words: 51
One-charged-wall electro-osmotic channel OurBigBook.com
Zero wall charge constrains the jump in normal electric displacement, while fixing a wall potential is a separate electrical condition. Taking the external normal field to vanish gives a zero normal derivative at an ideal uncharged wall. A grounded wall may carry induced charge even though its imposed potential is zero.

Differentiating the screened-channel velocity gives xmax​=d−κ−1arsinh[(coshκd−1)/(κd)]. For κd≫1, xmax​≃log(κd)/κ. The outer flow declines almost linearly to the passive no-slip wall rather than forming a symmetric plug.

Helmholtz-Smoluchowski electro-osmotic velocity (U=−εζE/η)

Words: 45
Electro-osmosis OurBigBook.com
In a half-space with no pressure gradient, Stokes balance and Poisson electrostatics give ηv′′=εEψ′′. No slip at the wall and zero bulk shear imply v=εE(ψ−ζ)/η. The bulk velocity is U=−εζE/η; it is not the fluid speed at the no-slip wall.

Coion

Words: 51
Electric double layer OurBigBook.com
A coion has electric charge of the same sign as the reference interface or particle. Its number density is depleted near that interface in the simplest Poisson-Boltzmann equation description. A counterion has the opposite sign. These roles depend on the reference charge: near a positively charged sphere in magnesium chloride, magnesium ions are coions and chloride ions are counterions.

Earnshaw's theorem

Words: 42
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
For a point electric charge in a charge-free neighbourhood, a static electric potential obeys Laplace's equation. The maximum principle for harmonic functions excludes a strict interior minimum or maximum of that electric potential, hence a strict minimum of the charge's potential energy. A static electric field alone therefore cannot provide stable three-dimensional confinement under these assumptions.

Faraday's ice pail experiment

Words: 886
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
Faraday's ice pail experiment distinguishes redistribution of electric charge by electrostatic induction from transfer of electric charge by contact. Lower a charged body into an initially neutral isolated metal pail: an externally connected electrometer responds even though the body never touches the metal. Withdraw the body without contact and the response disappears. Repeat with conductive contact before withdrawal and a residual response can remain. The striking point is that an exterior response does not establish that the pail has gained net electric charge.
Apparatus and readout. A modern implementation uses two concentric wire-mesh cylinders: a 10 cm diameter, 15 cm high inner pail on insulating rods and a grounded outer shield. Connect the electrometer's signal lead to the inner pail and its reference lead to the shield. Momentarily ground and zero the signal assembly, then isolate it; the shield remains grounded. A charged disk on an insulating handle goes into the lower half without touching. The electrometer measures electric potential difference in volts, with sign determined by the lead connections. It does not directly measure electric charge in coulombs.[ref]
A charge ledger before contact. To separate exact reasoning from the open apparatus, first idealize the pail as a closed cavity in a conductor with one internal body of total electric charge q. Let the isolated metal have total electric charge Q0​. The metal's electric field is zero at electrostatic equilibrium.[ref] A Gaussian surface enclosing the cavity in a conductor but lying wholly in the metal therefore has zero electric flux. Gauss's law and charge conservation give
q+Qinner​=0,Qinner​+Qouter​=Q0​,Qouter​=Q0​+q.
(2)
For Q0​=0 and q>0, the inner-wall total is −q and the outer-wall total is +q: the metal remains neutral. The exterior electric field can therefore be nonzero without any transfer from the body. The connected electrometer and signal cable belong to the same isolated conducting assembly and share its exterior electric charge. The zero-electric field assertion concerns metal, not the occupied cavity in a conductor.
This ledger fixes totals, not the local surface charge density. Moving an off-center body changes the inner-wall distribution while its integral remains −q. With fixed outer geometry, fixed Q0​+q and unchanged exterior sources, Uniqueness of the Dirichlet problem together with the fixed total outer electric charge determines the same exterior solution: the outside cannot reveal the body's position or detailed internal distribution. For example, internal bodies with stipulated electric charges +2q and −q give the same total exterior response as a single body with +q. Internal bodies with +q and −q can give a null exterior response while retaining a nonzero internal electric field. This is why a null reading cannot establish an empty cavity in a conductor.
Withdrawal is the control. Record a baseline, insert without contact, withdraw, and check return to baseline. After a fresh zero, repeat with the charged disk touching the inner wall, then withdraw and record the residual response. Finally zero the pail and reinsert the disk without contact to test remaining electric charge. Keep the operator grounded, discharge unwanted handle electric charge, and keep the unused charged disk distant. Dirty supports and humidity promote leakage. These controls separate transfer from electrostatic induction and stray coupling.[ref]
In the ideal contact test, the internal body is itself an electrical conductor and makes a conducting connection to the wall. After charge relaxation, body and enclosure become a single equipotential; the remaining charge-free void has zero electric field. The body then carries no excess electric charge on surfaces facing that void. Withdrawal without subsequent charging leaves total metal electric charge Q0​+q. A coated paddle can retain electric charge on insulating patches, so merely touching it does not guarantee complete transfer. A residual reading establishes some transfer under the controls; the disk retest checks the stronger claim of complete transfer. The ideal argument assumes no leakage and no relevant contact-generated charging.
Grounding changes the ledger. With no exterior sources and zero electric potential at infinity, a closed grounded enclosure has zero exterior electric field, inner-wall electric charge −q and zero outer-wall electric charge.[ref] Consequently, disconnecting ground before withdrawal retains total metal electric charge −q, which moves to the exterior after withdrawal. Keeping ground connected during withdrawal instead restores zero electric charge. A lasting opposite-sign response can therefore arise through grounding without body–wall contact.
For the real open pail, no Gaussian surface lying wholly in metal closes over the mouth. Increasing insertion depth and seeking a stable response tests whether enclosure is a good approximation; mesh openings, rim proximity and nearby objects limit it. In a fixed-geometry approximation, the positive insertion response obeys ΔV≃q/Ceff​, where Ceff​ is the effective capacitance of the pail, shield, cable and electrometer input. Changed geometry changes that conversion. Wait for charge relaxation and instrument settling at each step, while keeping the observation short compared with leakage. The experiment probes settled electrostatics; it does not establish shielding against arbitrary changing electromagnetic fields.

Electrostatic interface boundary conditions ([Dn​]=σfixed​)

Words: 65
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
Across a charged dielectric interface the tangential electric field is continuous and the normal displacement jump is the fixed surface charge density. Without a dipole sheet the electrostatic potential is continuous. For a charge sheet with equal permittivity on both sides, its normal potential derivative has jump −σfixed​/ε. Setting the field to zero on one side is an additional physical boundary assumption, as in a conductor or a negligible-exterior-admittance idealization.

Debye–Hückel approximation ((∇2−κD2​)ϕ=−ρfixed​/ε)

Words: 340 Articles: 4
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
The Debye–Hückel approximation linearizes mobile-ion Boltzmann densities about a neutral bulk electrolyte. It is valid for ionic potential energies small compared with kB​T. The inverse Debye–Hückel screening length satisfies κD2​=∑i​ni​zi2​e2/(εkB​T). The quadratic screened charging free energy includes both electric field energy and the linearized ionic-response term εκD2​ϕ2/2.

Planar Debye-Hückel double layer (ψ(x)=ψ0​e−κx,σ=εκψ0​)

Words: 100
Debye–Hückel approximation OurBigBook.com
For a plane bounding a symmetric electrolyte in x>0, assume no displacement field on the other side, bulk potential zero, and ∣zeψ∣≪kB​T. The Debye–Hückel approximation gives ψ′′=κ2ψ, whose decaying solution is ψ0​e−κx. The electrostatic interface boundary conditions give σ=−εψ′(0+)=εκψ0​. Equivalently, its diffuse charge density is ρe​=−εκ2ψ and its integral is −σ. Here ε=ε0​εr​ in SI units and κ2=2z2e2n∞​/(εkB​T) when n∞​ counts each ionic species. An isolated sheet with identical electrolyte on both sides has two diffuse layers, so the total sheet charge is 2εκψ0​ instead. A surface geometry and the field on its other side must therefore be specified.

Debye-Hückel potential of a charged sphere (ϕ(r)=Qe−κ(r−a)/[4πεr(1+κa)])

Words: 83
Debye–Hückel approximation OurBigBook.com
For a uniformly charged sphere of radius a, total electric charge Q, and an exterior dilute electrolyte of permittivity ε, the Debye–Hückel approximation gives (r2ϕ′)′=κ2r2ϕ. Decay at infinity and Gauss's law, −εϕ′(a)=Q/(4πa2), select the displayed electric potential. Substituting u=rϕ reduces the proof to u′′=κ2u. The screening parameter is κ2=∑i​zi2​e2ni,∞​/(εkB​T), and the ion profiles are ni​≃ni,∞​(1−zi​eϕ/(kB​T)). The validity condition is ∣zi​eϕ(a)∣≪kB​T for every relevant species. Integrating the diffuse charge density using the radial equation gives total screening charge −Q.

Debye–Hückel approximation OurBigBook.com
A lateral sinusoidal surface charge density with wave number k in the Debye–Hückel approximation generates vertical exponential or hyperbolic functions with inverse length p=k2+κD2​​. In a homogeneous electrolyte filling all space, an isolated sheet at zs​ produces ϕ=σk​(x)e−p∣z−zs​∣/(2εp). Boundary conditions determine the normalization when the electrolyte occupies only a gap.

Phase registration of screened charged sheets (θmin​=π(mod2π))

Words: 61
Screened sinusoidal surface-charge mode OurBigBook.com
Two equally modulated charge sheets in identical full-space electrolyte have charging energy per area α2[1+e−pdcosθ]/(4εp), where p=k2+κD2​​. Its phase-dependent interaction favors a half-wavelength offset, with opposite charge patches facing each other. For an electrolyte gap with negligible exterior displacement response, the energy is instead α2[coth(pd)+cosθ/sinh(pd)]/(2εp), with the same minimizing phase. Absolute energies require specified exterior electrostatic interface boundary conditions.

Bjerrum length (ℓB​)

Words: 53
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
For a chosen reference charge q, the separation at which its Coulomb interaction energy equals kB​T. The charge-q convention is ℓB​=q2/(4πϵabs​kB​T) in SI, or ℓB​=βq2/ϵ in Gaussian units. The commonly tabulated value uses the elementary charge; changing counterion valence requires tracking that reference convention. It sets the strength of counterion condensation.

Poisson-Boltzmann equation

Words: 905 Articles: 16
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
A mean-field coupling of the Poisson equation to an ideal Boltzmann distribution of mobile ions. In Gaussian units with uniform dielectric constant ϵ, ∇2ϕ=−(4π/ϵ)[ρf​+∑i​qi​ni,0​e−βqi​ϕ]. The potential reference and chemical potentials determine the normalization factors. It neglects discrete-ion correlations and assumes local thermal equilibrium. A counterion-only model is not the same equation as a symmetric salt reservoir.

Planar counterion-only double layer (n(z)=[2πℓB​(z+b)2]−1)

Words: 59
Poisson-Boltzmann equation OurBigBook.com
A negatively charged plane with monovalent positive counterions in z>0 and no salt reservoir has the mean-field profile displayed above, where b=e/(2πℓB​∣σ∣) and Bjerrum length ℓB​=e2/(4πεkB​T). Its potential relative to the wall is 2kB​Tlog(1+z/b)/e. The positive-ion charge density integrates to ∣σ∣, neutralizing the plane; the field decays algebraically. The potential has no finite zero-at-infinity reference, unlike the screened symmetric-reservoir problem.

Nonlinear planar Poisson-Boltzmann profile (u(z)=4artanh[tanh(u0​/4)e−κD​z])

Words: 70
Poisson-Boltzmann equation OurBigBook.com
For a symmetric monovalent point-ion electrolyte next to a plane, define u=eψ/(kB​T) and κD2​=2e2n∞​/(εkB​T), with n∞​ the density of each sign. The Poisson-Boltzmann equation becomes u′′=κD2​sinhu. Multiplying by u′ and matching zero field and potential in the bulk gives (u′)2=2κD2​(coshu−1). The decaying branch integrates to the displayed profile, reducing to u0​e−κD​z at weak potential. This solution assumes a salt reservoir and is distinct from a counterion-only diffuse layer.

Separating the pair from 0.20 to 0.40m therefore requires external work ΔU=+1.3485×10−7J if the initial and final kinetic energies agree; the electric force does −1.3485×10−7J of work. Separating them all the way to infinity requires +2.697×10−7J. The negative initial potential energy means that the pair lies below the chosen separated reference; it does not mean a negative kinetic energy.
Like-signed electric charges have positive U, which decreases as they separate, so their electric force is repulsive. Opposite-signed electric charges have negative U, which decreases as they approach, so their electric force is attractive. This attractive interaction supplies the Coulomb potential used in the hydrogen atom; determining its stationary quantum states also requires quantum mechanics. [ref]. Dividing U by a nonzero test electric charge q2​ gives the source's electric potential Φ1​=kq1​/r. More generally, the electrostatic potential energy of point charges sums each unordered charge pair once. This energy description is useful because work between two separations follows from endpoint values, without integrating a complicated trajectory.

Conductor in electrostatic equilibrium

Words: 2k Articles: 9
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an electrical conductor at rest whose mobile charge carriers have finished redistributing, with no maintained bulk electric current. In the ideal macroscopic model,
Emetal​=0,Φ=Vc​ on each connected conductor,ρmetal​=0.
(12)
A residual bulk electric field would drive further electric charge redistribution. The electric potential difference between any two points joined through the metal is −∫E⋅dl=0, so each connected piece is an equipotential. Gauss's law then gives zero net bulk charge density. This is a statement about net macroscopic electric charge, not the absence of positive atomic nuclei and negative electrons. Excess electric charge is represented by surface charge density; atomic surface structure is outside this continuum model. [ref].
The word inside must distinguish metal from a cavity in a conductor. A completely enclosed, charge-free cavity in a conductor has constant boundary electric potential Vc​. The constant solution of Laplace's equation and Uniqueness of the Dirichlet problem give Φ=Vc​ and E=0 throughout the cavity in a conductor, regardless of its shape or external electric charges. Grounding is unnecessary for this inward electrostatic shielding; an isolated enclosure can change its overall electric potential without producing an internal electric field. Zero enclosed net electric charge alone would only give zero electric flux. A positive and negative pair inside a cavity in a conductor can have zero total electric charge and a nonzero electric field. [ref].
If fixed electric charges inside a cavity in a conductor sum to q, a Gaussian surface lying entirely in the metal and enclosing that cavity in a conductor has zero electric flux. Thus the total induced inner-wall electric charge is −q. For one such cavity in a conductor and an isolated enclosure with total metal electric charge Qc​, the outer-wall electric charge is Qc​+q. In particular, an initially neutral isolated enclosure generally has an exterior electric field when q=0. For fixed internal sources, external changes only shift the constant electric potential inside an isolated enclosure, leaving the internal electric field unchanged. [ref].
A grounded enclosure fixes Vc​=0 and can acquire metal electric charge −q; with no exterior sources and Φ→0 at infinity, Uniqueness of the Dirichlet problem gives zero exterior electric field. With external sources present, the exterior electric field need not vanish, but it is independent of the internal sources at fixed grounded boundary electric potential. [ref].
Faraday's ice pail experiment makes the distinction between redistribution and transfer visible. In his letter of 4 February 1843, Faraday described an insulated pewter pail connected by wire to a gold-leaf electrometer, and a brass ball suspended on a long dry silk thread to reduce the hand's influence. He discharged the pail and charged the ball away from it. Lowering the ball without contact produced leaf divergence, which grew during entry and became approximately independent of further depth; withdrawing it collapsed the leaves. Contact with the bottom transferred electric charge, and the withdrawn ball was discharged. The readout was leaf divergence, not a direct map of the internal electric field. These observations distinguish electrostatic induction from contact transfer of electric charge. [ref].
For a modern version of Faraday's ice pail experiment, connect an insulated inner metal pail to the signal input of a high-input-impedance electrometer, with its reference lead and an outer shield grounded. Zero and momentarily ground the pail, then isolate the signal side. Lower a charged paddle deeply without touching and record the electric potential difference; withdraw it and check return to zero. Repeat with contact, then withdrawal: a residual reading indicates transferred electric charge. Reverse the paddle's sign and repeat. The electrometer reads volts; inferring electric charge requires the effective capacitance of pail, cable and input, so a stable reading at fixed geometry is a relative measure, not automatically a value in coulombs. Keep supports clean, nearby charged objects distant, and the operator grounded; humidity can cause leakage. [ref].
A complementary electrostatic shielding demonstration uses a charged hollow metal enclosure, a small metal sampling ball on an insulating handle, and an electrometer. Discharge the sampling ball between trials; touch it to the exterior, withdraw it, and transfer its collected electric charge to the electrometer. Repeat by touching the inner wall without touching the exterior during withdrawal. The exterior sample produces a response, whereas the inner sample gives a null within instrument sensitivity. This compares accessible surface responses rather than assuming a perfectly spherical enclosure. [ref]. Useful additional controls are an uncharged enclosure baseline, a repeat exterior sample to verify sensitivity, and repeated trials at different depths. An access hole, charged handle, leakage or disturbed surface charge density limits the inference; a null bounds detectable transfer, rather than proving an exactly zero electric field. An open pail's depth plateau tests good enclosure empirically. Neither demonstration establishes shielding of arbitrary time-dependent electromagnetic fields.

For radii a,λa,2a, the capacitance per unit length is the sum C′=2πϵ0​[1/logλ+1/log(2/λ)]. Writing u=logλ and L=log2, the function 1/u+1/(L−u) is strictly convex on (0,L) and symmetric about L/2. Hence C′ has its unique minimum at λ=2​, with value 8πϵ0​/log2. As λ=1+δ approaches the inner conductor, C′∼2πϵ0​/δ, agreeing with the local parallel-plate capacitor approximation.

Electric dipole moment

Words: 2k Articles: 14
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
The electric dipole moment measures the first spatial moment of signed electric charge. For localized point charges qi​ at positions ri​, or an integrable charge density ρ(r) with a finite first moment, define
p=∑i​qi​ri​,p=∫rρ(r)d3r,Q=∑i​qi​=∫ρ(r)d3r.
(24)
[ref].
The electric dipole moment is a vector with SI units Cm: coulombs times length in metres. Opposite electric charges can cancel in Q while contributing in the same direction to p. For a neutral pair with positive electric charge q>0 at r+​ and negative electric charge −q at r−​,
d=r+​−r−​,p=qd.
(25)
Thus the electric dipole moment points from negative to positive electric charge, not along the attraction between the two point charges. [ref].
Changing the coordinate origin changes the position vectors, not the physical electric charge distribution. If the new origin is at a relative to the old origin, ri′​=ri​−a, so direct substitution gives
p′=∑i​qi​(ri​−a)=p−Qa.
(26)
Consequently charge neutrality makes the electric dipole moment independent of the origin. For a system with nonzero total electric charge, always specify the origin: a single point charge at the old origin has p=0 but p′=−Qa. This is coordinate bookkeeping, not a newly created electric dipole. The full electric potential stays the same at the same physical point; the terms of its electric multipole expansion and the observation coordinates change together.
As a stipulated numerical example, put +2nC at (1,0,0)mm and −2nC at (−1,0,0)mm. Their total electric charge is zero and p=(4×10−12,0,0)Cm. Translating the origin by (3,−2,0)mm leaves this electric dipole moment unchanged. Adding +1nC at the old origin instead gives Q=1nC and p′=(1,2,0)×10−12Cm. Distinguishing these two cases prevents the mistaken claim that every electric dipole moment is independent of the origin.
The usefulness of the electric dipole moment is compression: many internal electric charges determine one vector governing the leading distant electric potential of a neutral localized object when p=0. [ref]. A polar molecule need not literally contain two point charges; its atomic nuclei and electron density collectively give an electric dipole moment. For example, the chemical polarity of water reflects its bent molecular geometry, whereas the symmetric linear molecular geometry of carbon dioxide makes its permanent electric dipole moment vanish. [ref]. A collection of such electric dipole moments per unit volume gives electric polarization. [ref].

Electric polarizability (dind​=αE)

Words: 528 Articles: 7
Electric dipole moment OurBigBook.com
Electric polarizability relates an induced electric dipole moment to an applied electric field. In a weak-field model with linearity, dind​=αE. A tensor response allows different electric field directions to induce electric dipole moments in different directions. A response that changes with molecular rotation enables rotational Raman spectroscopy.

Harmonic-oscillator electric polarizability (αel​=q2/k)

Words: 53
Electric polarizability OurBigBook.com
A bound charge in a harmonic restoring potential has induced electric dipole moment d=(q2/k)E. Completing the square proves this for every static field within the strictly harmonic model. First-order nondegenerate perturbation theory gives the same coefficient because the position operator connects the unperturbed ground state only to the first excited state. This exact response coefficient does not make its two-state wavefunction approximation exact.

Polarizability tensor (piinduced​=∑j​αij​Ej​)

Words: 74 Articles: 1
Electric polarizability OurBigBook.com
The linear response relating an induced electric dipole moment to an applied electric field. In ordinary nonresonant Raman spectroscopy, changes in its symmetric components during a normal mode determine activity. These components transform like x2,y2,z2,xy,xz,yz.
Rank-one needle polarizability (α∥​uuT)
Words: 45
Polarizability tensor OurBigBook.com
A slender high-permittivity particle responds mainly along its axis u, giving α≃α∥​uuT. Far-field projection into an observation plane leaves one real polarization direction. Every nonzero output is therefore linearly polarized in this leading approximation, even for circular or unpolarized input.

Dynamic electric polarizability (dω​=α(ω)Eω​)

Words: 203 Articles: 1
Electric polarizability OurBigBook.com
The dynamic electric polarizability relates the induced electric dipole moment at a driving frequency to the applied electric field at that frequency in linear response theory. A complex coefficient can encode both a dispersive phase and absorption. For a charged one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillator with charge magnitude e, mass m, and natural frequency ω0​, the undamped response is
α(ω)=m(ω02​−ω2)e2​.
(27)
One derivation uses the oscillator electric-dipole selection rule and first-order time-dependent perturbation theory. The same result follows from the classical Lorentz oscillator model: mz¨+mω02​z=−eE and d=−ez imply d¨+ω02​d=e2E/m. At exact resonance there is no bounded periodic response without damping; a finite switch-on produces secular growth rather than a finite steady-state value of the pole expression.
Harmonic-oscillator dipole response to switched radiation
Words: 100
Dynamic electric polarizability OurBigBook.com
For a localized quantum harmonic oscillator along z, let the transverse magnetic vector potential be Az​(t)=2A0​cos(θ−ωt) for t>0, with zero potential before the switch. The Coulomb gauge form of minimal coupling gives H1​=eAz​pz​/m. The creation operator matrix element ⟨1∣pz​∣0⟩=imℏω0​/2​ means that only ∣1⟩ is reached at first order from the ground state. Its interaction picture amplitude is
b1​=eA0​2mℏω0​​​[eiθFω0​−ω​(t)+e−iθFω0​+ω​(t)],Fν​(t)=∫0t​eiνt′dt′.
(28)
In particular F0​=t, so resonant finite-time expressions are nonsingular. The induced electric dipole moment is −2eℏ/(2mω0​)​Re(e−iω0​tb1​). It contains a driven component with the dynamic electric polarizability and free-frequency transients required by the initial conditions. The discontinuity in Az​ gives an impulsive electric field and an initial mechanical velocity eAz​(0+)/m even though the initial canonical momentum has zero mean.

Induced dipole moment and quadratic energy shift (δE=−21​αE2,d=αE)

Electric polarizability OurBigBook.com
For a nondegenerate parity-symmetric ground state in an external electric field, write the perturbation as V=−Ed^. The first-order state correction gives
⟨d^⟩=2E∑k=0​Ek(0)​−E0(0)​∣⟨k∣d^∣0⟩∣2​+O(E3)=αE+O(E3).
(29)
The positive coefficient α is the electric polarizability along the applied direction. Meanwhile second-order nondegenerate perturbation theory gives δE0(2)​=−αE2/2. Thus the induced electric dipole moment satisfies d=−2δE0(2)​/E, not −δE0(2)​/E. The Hellmann–Feynman theorem independently gives d=−∂E0​/∂E.
Charge-induced dipole attraction (U=−αQ2/[2(4πϵ0​)2r4])
Words: 100
Induced dipole moment and quadratic energy shift OurBigBook.com
A neutral isotropic atom with static electric polarizability α>0 in the field of a distant point charge Q has induced dipole p=αE and energy U=−αE2/2. Since E=∣Q∣/(4πϵ0​r2),
U(r)=−2(4πϵ0​)2r4αQ2​,Fr​=−drdU​=−(4πϵ0​)2r52αQ2​.
(30)
The negative radial force is attractive for either sign of Q. Reversing Q reverses the induced dipole but not the energy or leading force. The factor 1/2 accounts for the work of inducing the dipole; using the permanent-dipole energy −p⋅E without that work would double the answer. The approximation assumes weak fields, a slowly varying field across the atom and negligible electronic overlap.

Electric dipole

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Electric dipole moment OurBigBook.com
A finite electric dipole consists of equal and opposite electric charges separated by a nonzero displacement. It has charge neutrality but a nonzero electric dipole moment p=qd. An ideal point electric dipole is the mathematical limit d=∣d∣→0 with p fixed, so q must increase as 1/d. Shrinking the separation while holding q fixed instead makes the electric dipole moment vanish. The ideal electric dipole describes an exterior electric field; it does not reproduce the two near-charge singularities or the internal structure of a molecule. [ref].
Place the pair's midpoint at the origin and write ke​=1/(4πϵ0​), where ϵ0​ is vacuum permittivity. By superposition principle and Coulomb's law, its exact electric potential away from the two point charges is
Φpair​(r)=ke​q(∣r−d/2∣1​−∣r+d/2∣1​).
(32)
For r=∣r∣≫d, retain the first nonzero term of a Taylor series. The electric potential and its negative gradient become
Φdip​(r)=ke​r2p⋅r​,Edip​(r)=r3ke​​[3(p⋅r)r−p],r>0.
(33)
Here r=r/r and the products in parentheses are dot products. These are exact exterior formulas for the ideal electric dipole and distant approximations for a finite pair. The electric field on the outer axis points along p with magnitude 2ke​p/r3; on the perpendicular bisector it points opposite p with magnitude ke​p/r3. This directional structure is what a scalar total electric charge misses. [ref].
In a prescribed uniform external electric field Eext​, a rigid pair has opposite forces F±​=±qEext​. Its net force is zero, but summing their moments about the midpoint gives the torque
τ=2d​×qEext​+(−2d​)×(−qEext​)=p×Eext​.
(34)
The cross product makes the torque perpendicular to both the electric dipole moment and the external electric field. If θ is the angle from Eext​ to p in their plane, the signed turning torque is τθ​=−pEext​sinθ. It tends to reduce a small positive θ. [ref].
The external interaction potential energy, with zero chosen at θ=π/2, is
U=−p⋅Eext​=−pEext​cosθ,τθ​=−dθdU​.
(35)
Parallel alignment minimizes this potential energy; antiparallel alignment maximizes it even though the torque is zero in both positions. This omits the pair's constant internal binding potential energy and assumes a fixed permanent electric dipole moment. [ref].
A nonuniform external electric field can exert a net force on a neutral electric dipole. Before taking the small-pair approximation, the exact external force is F=q[Eext​(R+d/2)−Eext​(R−d/2)], where R is the midpoint. A first-order Taylor series gives, for a fixed electric dipole moment and an external electric field varying slowly across d,
F≃(p⋅∇)Eext​=∇(p⋅Eext​)
(36)
in electrostatics. The last equality uses the vanishing curl of the external electric field, with p held fixed while differentiating. Thus uniform external electric fields turn a misaligned electric dipole, whereas gradients can also move its midpoint. For example, the local source-free electric field Eext​=Gxx+(E0​−Gy)y​ gives F=(Gpx​,−Gpy​,0), so reversing the electric dipole moment reverses the net force. This stipulated local model has zero divergence and zero curl.
A motivating experiment is Filsinger and colleagues' study of electrostatic deflection of polar molecules. Benzonitrile (C7​H5​N) in helium expanded from a pulsed valve into vacuum; two 1-mm skimmers narrowed the beam before a 15-cm deflector. A grounded trough and a high-voltage rod produced a vertical electric field gradient. Scanning a focused laser vertically downstream and recording benzonitrile ions from photoionization measured the beam's relative density. With voltage off, the profile spanned about 2 mm; applying voltage shifted and broadened it upwards. At 10 kV, many molecules lay outside the original profile. [ref].
Interpretation uses a quantum state's Stark effect energy W(E): μeff​=−dW/dE gives Fy​=μeff​∂y​E. States whose energy falls with increasing electric field seek stronger fields. The voltage-off profile controls the mechanical aperture. Inferring state populations needs calculated trajectories, speed distributions and a rotational temperature model; profile displacement alone does not measure a permanent electric dipole moment uniquely. This is an electric Stark effect experiment, with photoionization occurring after deflection. [ref].
For the symmetric finite pair, the first omitted electric multipole expansion term after the electric dipole is third order, so typical relative errors scale as (d/r)2. This stronger error estimate need not hold for an arbitrary neutral molecule with a nonzero electric quadrupole moment. A concrete check for a pair on the z axis compares the exact and ideal electric fields at r>d/2 on the positive axis and at r>0 on the perpendicular bisector:
Ez,dip​(0,0,r)Ez,pair​(0,0,r)​=(1−4r2d2​)−2,Ez,dip​(r,0,0)Ez,pair​(r,0,0)​=(1+4r2d2​)−3/2.
(37)
Both perpendicular-bisector components are negative. At r=5d, the ratios are approximately 1.0203 and 0.9852: errors of +2.03% and −1.48% relative to the ideal electric field. The condition r≫d concerns observing the pair's own electric field; the separate condition for its external force approximation concerns variation of the applied electric field across the pair.

Electric dipole field (E=[3(p⋅r^)r^−p]/(4πϵ0​r3))

Words: 75
Electric dipole OurBigBook.com
At distances large compared with the separation of a neutral charge pair, its electric field has the displayed leading form in terms of the electric dipole moment p. Measure the polar angle from p. The radial and angular components are Er​=2pcosθ/(4πϵ0​r3) and Eθ​=psinθ/(4πϵ0​r3), giving ∣E∣=p1+3cos2θ​/(4πϵ0​r3). At fixed radius the polar field magnitude is twice the equatorial one. This leading neutral-pair field falls as r−3, faster than the r−2 electric field of an isolated point charge.

r3p1​⋅p2​​−r53(p1​⋅r)(p2​⋅r)​.

Transverse electric-dipole pair energy
Words: 54
Electric dipole-dipole interaction OurBigBook.com
The point-dipole energy is [p1​⋅p2​−3(p1​⋅r^)(p2​⋅r^)]/(4πϵ0​r3). If the separation is perpendicular to the first dipole, the second term vanishes. Parallel dipoles then have positive energy p1​p2​/(4πϵ0​r3), while mutually perpendicular dipoles give zero in this approximation. Real molecular interactions can include multipoles, induction and short-range contributions beyond this point-dipole term.

Electric multipole expansion

Words: 272 Articles: 6
Electrostatics OurBigBook.com
For a localized charge distribution, the far electric potential is an inverse-radius expansion whose first terms are the total charge monopole, the electric dipole moment, and the electric quadrupole moment.

Electric quadrupole moment (Qij​=∑a​qa​(3ra,i​ra,j​−∣ra​∣2δij​))

Words: 67
Electric multipole expansion OurBigBook.com
The trace-free electric quadrupole moment is a symmetric tensor measuring the second-order term in an electric multipole expansion. For a localized charge distribution its contribution to the far-field electrostatic potential is Qij​ri​rj​/(8πϵ0​r3), with summation over indices. The moment may be nonzero even when the total electric charge or electric dipole moment is nonzero; it should not be confused with an electric quadrupole whose lower moments vanish. Changing the origin generally changes the tensor when lower moments are nonzero.

Electric quadrupole

Words: 87 Articles: 1
Electric multipole expansion OurBigBook.com
An electric quadrupole is a charge distribution whose total charge and electric dipole moment vanish while its second charge moment does not. Its potential decays as r−3.

Planar quadrupole potential (V=A(x2−y2),E=(−2Ax,2Ay,0))

Words: 62
Electric quadrupole OurBigBook.com
This electric potential is harmonic and independent of z. Its electric field is linear in transverse position, with a saddle at the origin. For A>0, field lines approach along the x axis and leave along the y axis; off-axis field lines satisfy xy=constant. Equipotentials satisfy x2−y2=constant. This is a local planar electric quadrupole geometry, not the decaying far field of an isolated three-dimensional quadrupole.

The monopole vanishes when N=M+1, the dipole vanishes when M=1, and both vanish when (N,M)=(2,1).
